questions.question: When are two systems of equations equivalent?
options: When they have the same solution set.
When their equations are written in the same order.
When they contain the same number of symbols.
When their coefficient matrices have the same entries regardless of right-hand side.

questions.question: Why can equivalent systems look different?
options: They have no equations left after solving.
Equivalent systems must look identical once the equations are put in the same order
They may encode the same solution set with different equations
Each equation must be nonlinear.

questions.question: What do elementary row operations preserve when applied to a system?
options: The order of unknowns only.
The solution set.
The individual equation text.
The number of nonzero coefficients in each row.

questions.question: What does elimination do to a system conceptually?
options: It turns every system into a homogeneous system.
It replaces it by easier equivalent systems.
It changes the solution set to make solving possible.
It deletes the right-hand side vector.

questions.question: Does swapping the order of equations change the solution set?
options: No, but only for equations in one variable.
Yes, unless the system is homogeneous.
No, it gives an equivalent system.
Yes, the first equation is always more important.

questions.question: Which system is equivalent to $x+y=2$, $x-y=0$?
Which operation clearly gives an equivalent system?
options: Deleting an equation without justification.
Changing the right-hand side from $2$ to $3$.
Swapping the first and second equations.
Replacing one equation by $0=1$.

questions.question: Are the systems $x=1$, $y=2$ and $y=2$, $x=1$ equivalent?
options: Yes, they have the same solution set.
No, the first variables differ.
Yes, but only if $x=y$.
No, the equations are in a different order.

questions.question: Which system is not equivalent to $x=0$?
Replacing $x+y=2$ by $2x+2y=4$ gives what kind of equation?
options: A nonlinear equation.
A contradictory equation.
An equation with no variables.
An equivalent equation.

questions.question: Why is “same number of equations” not enough for equivalence?
options: Equivalence also requires identical coefficients in every equation.
Equivalence is decided by the number of unknowns rather than equations.
Two systems of the same size can still have different solution sets.
Equivalence also requires the equations to be listed in the same order.

questions.question: Why is row reduction useful for solving systems?
options: It changes difficult solution sets into simpler different ones.
It keeps the solution set while making the equations easier to read.
It removes all variables from the system.
It only works when the original system has no solutions.

questions.question: If two systems are equivalent and one has no solution, what about the other?
options: It must be homogeneous.
It must have infinitely many solutions.
It also has no solution.
It must have exactly one solution.

questions.question: Which system is equivalent to $x+y=3$, $x-y=1$ after adding the first equation to the second?
Are $x+y=2$ and $2x+2y=5$ equivalent as single equations?
options: Yes, both contain $x+y$.
Yes, because both are linear.
No, because one equation has larger coefficients.
No, their solution sets are different.

questions.question: Which replacement preserves equivalence for the system with rows $R_1,R_2$?
options: $R_2\leftarrow 0R_2$.
$R_2\leftarrow R_2-3R_1$.
$R_1\leftarrow$ a row of arbitrary numbers.
Delete $R_1$.

questions.question: Why can a system be equivalent to one with an equation like $0=0$ added?
options: Adding any linear equation, not only $0=0$, keeps the system equivalent.
Adding $0=0$ fixes one free variable at $0$, which keeps the system consistent.
Adding $0=0$ preserves equivalence only if the system already has a zero row.
The equation $0=0$ imposes no extra restriction on solutions.

questions.question: When can deleting an equation preserve equivalence?
options: When the deleted equation is homogeneous, with right-hand side $0$.
When the deleted equation is implied by the remaining equations.
When the remaining system still has as many equations as unknowns.
When the remaining equations still have at least one common solution.

questions.question: Which single equation is equivalent to the system $x+y=2$, $2x+2y=4$?
The system $x+y=1$, $2x+2y=2$ is changed to $x+y=1$, $0=0$. What happened?
options: A nonlinear equation was introduced.
Subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives an equivalent system
The system became inconsistent.
The solution set changed from infinitely many solutions to the empty set, since $0=0$ says nothing
